claims.text: The starting material contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
Traditionally processed or operationally cycled W–Cu composites exhibit phase segregation.
Traditionally processed or operationally cycled W–Cu composites form voids at W–Cu interfaces.
The proposed intervention is a one-step HPHT post-treatment of the W–Cu composite.
HPHT treatment will densify the W–Cu microstructure.
HPHT treatment will promote controlled interdiffusion across W–Cu interfaces.
HPHT treatment will enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding and produce a more continuous interface.
High pressure reduces free volume at the interface.
High pressure suppresses the nucleation and growth of interfacial voids during high-temperature processing.
Elevated temperature promotes W–Cu interfacial diffusion that homogenizes the interface.
The combined pressure and temperature effects limit phase separation in W–Cu.
The combined pressure and temperature effects limit interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
A better-bonded, less-voided W–Cu interface reduces thermal barriers.
The improved interface will maintain high thermal conductivity despite irradiation-induced defect production.
After simulated irradiation and heat-transfer cycling, HPHT-treated W–Cu will have a significantly lower interfacial void fraction than untreated W–Cu.
After simulated irradiation and heat-transfer cycling, HPHT-treated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu.
Plasma-facing fusion components encounter severe heat, particle fluxes, and irradiation damage.
The proposed benefit depends on keeping temperature, pressure, duration, and atmosphere within limits that avoid melting and deleterious reactions.
